DANDU BALA VAMSI 
                 balavamsidandu@gmail.com| github.com/vamsidandu06 | Vamsidandu06 |+91-82475-44524 | India 
 
PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY 
Computer Science undergraduate pursuing a Bachelor of Technology (B. Tech) with a strong foundation in software 
engineering, data structures, algorithms, and object-oriented programming. Hands-on experience developing 
applications using Java and Python, building RESTful APIs, and collaborating in team-based environments. 
Demonstrates a growth mindset, strong problem-solving skills, and eagerness to learn through mentorship while 
contributing to real-world software engineering projects 
SKILLS 
Programming: Java, Python, C 
Web: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Node.js 
Databases: MySQL, MongoDB 
AI/ML: Machine Learning Fundamentals, LLM-based Systems 
Tools: Git, GitHub, Docker, FastAPI, VS Code, Eclipse, Jupyter Notebook 
WORK EXPERIENCE 
Engineering Projects (Academic) | University Coursework (2024 – Present) 
• Designed, developed, and tested software applications using Java, Python, and web technologies. 
• Collaborated on team projects to analyze requirements, implement features, and debug systems. 
• Applied data structures, algorithms, and object-oriented principles to solve technical problems. 
• Debugged and optimized code to improve performance and maintainability. 
PROJECTS 
Automated Interview and Grading System | Python, AI/ML (Oct 2025 – Present) 
• Built an AI-powered mock interview platform using LLMs for resume analysis and answer grading. 
• Implemented backend services using FastAPI and integrated Google Speech-to-Text. 
• Focused on modular design, scalability, and clean API architecture. 
 
ATM Management System | Java, MySQL (May 2025 – Sept 2025) 
• Developed a secure ATM simulation supporting balance inquiry, withdrawals, and fund transfers. 
• Ensured system stability through debugging and testing. 
• Tested and debugged transaction logic to ensure reliability and accuracy. 
 
Time Table Automation System | Python, HTML, CSS, Bootstrap (Nov 2024 – Feb 2025) 
• Automated timetable generation to improve faculty and student scheduling efficiency. 
• Designed a user-friendly interface and implemented backend logic. 
• Improved scheduling efficiency through rule-based automation 
EDUCATION 
B.Tech in Computer Science and Engineering 
Vignan’s Foundation for Science, Technology & Research (2024 – 2028) 
CGPA: 8.2 / 10

answers.candidateAnswer:
To prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, you must ensure that no information from the test or validation dataset is available during model training or feature engineering. 

First, the train/test split must occur before ANY preprocessing or feature transformations. If you fit a StandardScaler, Imputer, or TargetEncoder on the entire dataset, validation information leaks into the training pipeline. In scikit-learn, this is avoided by strictly encapsulating transformers and estimators inside a Pipeline object and calling fit_transform only on training splits.

Second, for time-series or sequential data, random k-fold cross-validation will cause temporal leakage (predicting past events using future context). Instead, time-series split or rolling window validation must be utilized.

Third, group-level leakage must be mitigated using GroupKFold when multiple samples belong to the same entity (e.g. medical patients or user accounts) so that an entity doesn't appear in both train and validation splits.

evaluation.recommendedFollowUp: Escalate to advanced production system design or database architecture.

answers.candidateAnswer:
To prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, you must ensure that no information from the test or validation dataset is available during model training or feature engineering. 

First, the train/test split must occur before ANY preprocessing or feature transformations. If you fit a StandardScaler, Imputer, or TargetEncoder on the entire dataset, validation information leaks into the training pipeline. In scikit-learn, this is avoided by strictly encapsulating transformers and estimators inside a Pipeline object and calling fit_transform only on training splits.

Second, for time-series or sequential data, random k-fold cross-validation will cause temporal leakage (predicting past events using future context). Instead, time-series split or rolling window validation must be utilized.

Third, group-level leakage must be mitigated using GroupKFold when multiple samples belong to the same entity (e.g. medical patients or user accounts) so that an entity doesn't appear in both train and validation splits.

A hash map provides average O(1) time complexity for insertions and lookups by using a hash function to map keys to bucket indices in an underlying array.

Under the hood:
1. When a key is inserted, a hash function computes an integer hash code from the key, which is then mapped to a bucket index using modulo arithmetic: index = hash(key) % array_capacity.
2. In the average case, keys distribute uniformly across buckets, allowing constant-time direct array indexing.
3. However, hash collisions inevitably occur when two distinct keys yield the same index. There are two primary strategies to resolve this:
   - Separate Chaining: Each bucket stores a linked list (or balanced red-black tree, like Java 8+ HashMap when bucket size exceeds 8) of colliding entries.
   - Open Addressing: All entries reside directly in the array; upon collision, we probe alternative buckets using linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing.
4. If too many collisions occur without resizing, lookup degrades to O(n) worst-case. To prevent this, hash maps track a load factor (e.g. 0.75) and dynamically double the capacity and rehash all keys when exceeded.

To prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, you must ensure that no information from the test or validation dataset is available during model training or feature engineering. 

First, the train/test split must occur before ANY preprocessing or feature transformations. If you fit a StandardScaler, Imputer, or TargetEncoder on the entire dataset, validation information leaks into the training pipeline. Second, for time-series or sequential data, random k-fold cross-validation will cause temporal leakage (predicting past events using future context). Instead, time-series split or rolling window validation must be utilized.

Third, group-level leakage must be mitigated using GroupKFold when multiple samples belong to the same entity (e.g. medical patients or user accounts) so that an entity doesn't appear in both train and validation splits.

assessmentRecords.questionPrompt: Explain how you would prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, and describe the specific architectural patterns or code practices you use.
assessmentRecords.rubricCriteria: 1. Explains why preprocessing/scaling must occur after split or inside pipelines. 2. Identifies temporal/time-series leakage and appropriate splits. 3. Identifies group/entity leakage patterns.
assessmentRecords.whyThisQuestion: Selected as primary question because candidate's resume prominently claims experience in 'automated training pipelines preventing feature leakage', which directly matches the target job's high-importance requirement.
assessmentRecords.candidateAnswer:
To prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, you must ensure that no information from the test or validation dataset is available during model training or feature engineering. 

First, the train/test split must occur before ANY preprocessing or feature transformations. If you fit a StandardScaler, Imputer, or TargetEncoder on the entire dataset, validation information leaks into the training pipeline. In scikit-learn, this is avoided by strictly encapsulating transformers and estimators inside a Pipeline object and calling fit_transform only on training splits.

Second, for time-series or sequential data, random k-fold cross-validation will cause temporal leakage (predicting past events using future context). Instead, time-series split or rolling window validation must be utilized.

Third, group-level leakage must be mitigated using GroupKFold when multiple samples belong to the same entity (e.g. medical patients or user accounts) so that an entity doesn't appear in both train and validation splits.

supportingExcerpts: train/test split must occur before ANY preprocessing
evaluation.assessmentExplanation: Candidate demonstrated comprehensive technical understanding of data leakage vectors, pipeline encapsulation, and temporal split validation strategies with clear practical application.
evaluation.recommendedFollowUp: Escalate to advanced production system design or database architecture.

assessmentRecords.questionPrompt: Explain how you would prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, and describe the specific architectural patterns or code practices you use.
assessmentRecords.rubricCriteria: 1. Explains why preprocessing/scaling must occur after split or inside pipelines. 2. Identifies temporal/time-series leakage and appropriate splits. 3. Identifies group/entity leakage patterns.
assessmentRecords.whyThisQuestion: Selected as primary question because candidate's resume prominently claims experience in 'automated training pipelines preventing feature leakage', which directly matches the target job's high-importance requirement.
assessmentRecords.candidateAnswer:
To prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, you must ensure that no information from the test or validation dataset is available during model training or feature engineering. 

First, the train/test split must occur before ANY preprocessing or feature transformations. If you fit a StandardScaler, Imputer, or TargetEncoder on the entire dataset, validation information leaks into the training pipeline. In scikit-learn, this is avoided by strictly encapsulating transformers and estimators inside a Pipeline object and calling fit_transform only on training splits.

Second, for time-series or sequential data, random k-fold cross-validation will cause temporal leakage (predicting past events using future context). Instead, time-series split or rolling window validation must be utilized.

Third, group-level leakage must be mitigated using GroupKFold when multiple samples belong to the same entity (e.g. medical patients or user accounts) so that an entity doesn't appear in both train and validation splits.

assessmentRecords.questionPrompt: Explain how you would prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, and describe the specific architectural patterns or code practices you use.
assessmentRecords.rubricCriteria: 1. Explains why preprocessing/scaling must occur after split or inside pipelines. 2. Identifies temporal/time-series leakage and appropriate splits. 3. Identifies group/entity leakage patterns.
assessmentRecords.whyThisQuestion: Selected as primary question because candidate's resume prominently claims experience in 'automated training pipelines preventing feature leakage', which directly matches the target job's high-importance requirement.
assessmentRecords.candidateAnswer:
To prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, you must ensure that no information from the test or validation dataset is available during model training or feature engineering. 

First, the train/test split must occur before ANY preprocessing or feature transformations. If you fit a StandardScaler, Imputer, or TargetEncoder on the entire dataset, validation information leaks into the training pipeline. In scikit-learn, this is avoided by strictly encapsulating transformers and estimators inside a Pipeline object and calling fit_transform only on training splits.

Second, for time-series or sequential data, random k-fold cross-validation will cause temporal leakage (predicting past events using future context). Instead, time-series split or rolling window validation must be utilized.

Third, group-level leakage must be mitigated using GroupKFold when multiple samples belong to the same entity (e.g. medical patients or user accounts) so that an entity doesn't appear in both train and validation splits.

assessmentRecords.questionPrompt: Explain how you would prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, and describe the specific architectural patterns or code practices you use.
assessmentRecords.rubricCriteria: 1. Explains why preprocessing/scaling must occur after split or inside pipelines. 2. Identifies temporal/time-series leakage and appropriate splits. 3. Identifies group/entity leakage patterns.
assessmentRecords.whyThisQuestion: Selected as primary question because candidate's resume prominently claims experience in 'automated training pipelines preventing feature leakage', which directly matches the target job's high-importance requirement.
assessmentRecords.candidateAnswer:
To prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, you must ensure that no information from the test or validation dataset is available during model training or feature engineering. 

First, the train/test split must occur before ANY preprocessing or feature transformations. If you fit a StandardScaler, Imputer, or TargetEncoder on the entire dataset, validation information leaks into the training pipeline. In scikit-learn, this is avoided by strictly encapsulating transformers and estimators inside a Pipeline object and calling fit_transform only on training splits.

Second, for time-series or sequential data, random k-fold cross-validation will cause temporal leakage (predicting past events using future context). Instead, time-series split or rolling window validation must be utilized.

Third, group-level leakage must be mitigated using GroupKFold when multiple samples belong to the same entity (e.g. medical patients or user accounts) so that an entity doesn't appear in both train and validation splits.

supportingExcerpts: train/test split must occur before ANY preprocessing

evaluation.recommendedFollowUp: Escalate to advanced production system design or database architecture.

assessmentRecords.questionPrompt: Explain how you would prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, and describe the specific architectural patterns or code practices you use.
assessmentRecords.rubricCriteria: 1. Explains why preprocessing/scaling must occur after split or inside pipelines. 2. Identifies temporal/time-series leakage and appropriate splits. 3. Identifies group/entity leakage patterns.
assessmentRecords.whyThisQuestion: Selected as primary question because candidate's resume prominently claims experience in 'automated training pipelines preventing feature leakage', which directly matches the target job's high-importance requirement.
assessmentRecords.candidateAnswer:
To prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, you must ensure that no information from the test or validation dataset is available during model training or feature engineering. 

First, the train/test split must occur before ANY preprocessing or feature transformations. If you fit a StandardScaler, Imputer, or TargetEncoder on the entire dataset, validation information leaks into the training pipeline. In scikit-learn, this is avoided by strictly encapsulating transformers and estimators inside a Pipeline object and calling fit_transform only on training splits.

Second, for time-series or sequential data, random k-fold cross-validation will cause temporal leakage (predicting past events using future context). Instead, time-series split or rolling window validation must be utilized.

Third, group-level leakage must be mitigated using GroupKFold when multiple samples belong to the same entity (e.g. medical patients or user accounts) so that an entity doesn't appear in both train and validation splits.

To prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, you must ensure that no information from the test or validation dataset is available during model training or feature engineering.

assessmentRecords.questionPrompt: Explain the internal mechanics of a Hash Map. How does it achieve average O(1) lookup time, and what strategies are used to resolve hash collisions?
assessmentRecords.rubricCriteria: Level 4: Explains hash code calculation, bucket indexing via modulo, O(1) average vs O(n) worst case, and compares collision strategies (separate chaining vs open addressing). Level 2: Explains key-value lookup without collision handling. Level 1: Superficial explanation.
assessmentRecords.whyThisQuestion: Selected as primary question because Data Structures is the highest-priority competency for the Junior Software Engineer role, and the candidate's resume prominently claims implementation of a custom key-value store with collision handling.
assessmentRecords.candidateAnswer:
A hash map provides average O(1) time complexity for insertions and lookups by using a hash function to map keys to bucket indices in an underlying array.

Under the hood:
1. When a key is inserted, a hash function computes an integer hash code from the key, which is then mapped to a bucket index using modulo arithmetic: index = hash(key) % array_capacity.
2. In the average case, keys distribute uniformly across buckets, allowing constant-time direct array indexing.
3. However, hash collisions inevitably occur when two distinct keys yield the same index. There are two primary strategies to resolve this:
   - Separate Chaining: Each bucket stores a linked list (or balanced red-black tree, like Java 8+ HashMap when bucket size exceeds 8) of colliding entries.
   - Open Addressing: All entries reside directly in the array; upon collision, we probe alternative buckets using linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing.
4. If too many collisions occur without resizing, lookup degrades to O(n) worst-case. To prevent this, hash maps track a load factor (e.g. 0.75) and dynamically double the capacity and rehash all keys when exceeded.

assessmentRecords.questionPrompt: Explain the internal mechanics of a Hash Map. How does it achieve average O(1) lookup time, and what strategies are used to resolve hash collisions?
assessmentRecords.rubricCriteria: Level 4: Explains hash code calculation, bucket indexing via modulo, O(1) average vs O(n) worst case, and compares collision strategies (separate chaining vs open addressing). Level 2: Explains key-value lookup without collision handling. Level 1: Superficial explanation.
assessmentRecords.whyThisQuestion: Selected as primary question because Data Structures is the highest-priority competency for the Junior Software Engineer role, and the candidate's resume prominently claims implementation of a custom key-value store with collision handling.
assessmentRecords.candidateAnswer:
A hash map provides average O(1) time complexity for insertions and lookups by using a hash function to map keys to bucket indices in an underlying array.

Under the hood:
1. When a key is inserted, a hash function computes an integer hash code from the key, which is then mapped to a bucket index using modulo arithmetic: index = hash(key) % array_capacity.
2. In the average case, keys distribute uniformly across buckets, allowing constant-time direct array indexing.
3. However, hash collisions inevitably occur when two distinct keys yield the same index. There are two primary strategies to resolve this:
   - Separate Chaining: Each bucket stores a linked list (or balanced red-black tree, like Java 8+ HashMap when bucket size exceeds 8) of colliding entries.
   - Open Addressing: All entries reside directly in the array; upon collision, we probe alternative buckets using linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing.
4. If too many collisions occur without resizing, lookup degrades to O(n) worst-case. To prevent this, hash maps track a load factor (e.g. 0.75) and dynamically double the capacity and rehash all keys when exceeded.

assessmentRecords.questionPrompt: Explain how you would prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, and describe the specific architectural patterns or code practices you use.
assessmentRecords.rubricCriteria: Level 4: Explains why preprocessing must occur after split or inside pipelines. Identifies temporal/time-series leakage and group/entity leakage patterns. Level 2: Mentions train/test split without transformer encapsulation. Level 1: Superficial explanation.
assessmentRecords.whyThisQuestion: Why this question? Candidate's resume claims experience in automated training pipelines preventing feature leakage. This validates production data hygiene.
assessmentRecords.candidateAnswer:
To prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, you must ensure that no information from the test or validation dataset is available during model training or feature engineering. 

First, the train/test split must occur before ANY preprocessing or feature transformations. If you fit a StandardScaler, Imputer, or TargetEncoder on the entire dataset, validation information leaks into the training pipeline. In scikit-learn, this is avoided by strictly encapsulating transformers and estimators inside a Pipeline object and calling fit_transform only on training splits.

Second, for time-series or sequential data, random k-fold cross-validation will cause temporal leakage (predicting past events using future context). Instead, time-series split or rolling window validation must be utilized.

Third, group-level leakage must be mitigated using GroupKFold when multiple samples belong to the same entity (e.g. medical patients or user accounts) so that an entity doesn't appear in both train and validation splits.

To prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, you must ensure that no information from the test or validation dataset is available during model training or feature engineering.

assessmentRecords.questionPrompt: Explain how you would prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, and describe the specific architectural patterns or code practices you use.
assessmentRecords.rubricCriteria: Level 4: Explains why preprocessing must occur after split or inside pipelines. Identifies temporal/time-series leakage and group/entity leakage patterns. Level 2: Mentions train/test split without transformer encapsulation. Level 1: Superficial explanation.
assessmentRecords.whyThisQuestion: Why this question? Candidate's resume claims experience in automated training pipelines preventing feature leakage. This validates production data hygiene.
assessmentRecords.candidateAnswer:
To prevent data leakage when training a machine learning model, you must ensure that no information from the test or validation dataset is available during model training or feature engineering. 

First, the train/test split must occur before ANY preprocessing or feature transformations. If you fit a StandardScaler, Imputer, or TargetEncoder on the entire dataset, validation information leaks into the training pipeline. In scikit-learn, this is avoided by strictly encapsulating transformers and estimators inside a Pipeline object and calling fit_transform only on training splits.

Second, for time-series or sequential data, random k-fold cross-validation will cause temporal leakage (predicting past events using future context). Instead, time-series split or rolling window validation must be utilized.

Third, group-level leakage must be mitigated using GroupKFold when multiple samples belong to the same entity (e.g. medical patients or user accounts) so that an entity doesn't appear in both train and validation splits.

candidates.name: David Chen
candidates.resumeText:
DAVID CHEN
Junior Software Engineer | david.chen@alumni.edu | San Jose, CA | linkedin.com/in/davidchen-dev

SUMMARY
Motivated Software Engineer graduate with a strong foundation in data structures, algorithms, object-oriented design, and relational database systems. Proficient in Python, Java, SQL, and Git.

TECHNICAL SKILLS
- Languages: Python, Java, JavaScript, SQL, C++
- Data Structures & Algorithms: Hash Tables, Trees, Graphs, Sorting, Dynamic Programming
- Databases: PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL
- Core Concepts: Object-Oriented Design, RESTful APIs, Version Control (Git), Unit Testing

EDUCATION
B.S. in Computer Science | State University (Graduated May 2025)
- Relevant Coursework: Data Structures & Algorithms (Grade: A), Database Management Systems (Grade: A-), Operating Systems, Software Engineering

PROJECTS
- Distributed Key-Value Store: Implemented an in-memory key-value store in Python utilizing custom hash tables with separate chaining for collision resolution and LRU cache eviction.
- Student Enrollment Portal: Built a full-stack CRUD application with React and PostgreSQL, creating normalized schemas and indexed queries.

INTERNSHIP EXPERIENCE
Software Engineering Intern | TechStart Labs (Summer 2024)
- Implemented automated test suites and optimized database queries for internal analytics.
- Authored clear technical documentation and participated in daily standups and sprint retrospectives.

resumeClaims.claim: Implemented an in-memory key-value store in Python utilizing custom hash tables with separate chaining for collision resolution.
Strong foundation in data structures, algorithms, and computational complexity (Grade A in DSA).
Built a full-stack CRUD application with React and PostgreSQL, creating normalized schemas and indexed queries.
Authored clear technical documentation and participated in daily standups and sprint retrospectives.

candidates.recruiterNotes: Exceptional grasp of hash map internals and collision resolution. Solid potential for junior backend systems.
